paper_title: RealMe: Immersive Volumetric Video from Minimal Captures

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: This paper addresses the problem of creating immersive volumetric videos from sparse and low-resolution capture resources. Conventional dense multi-view reconstruction methods can produce high-quality volumetric videos, but their reliance on costly capture setups makes them impractical in real-world scenarios. Recent approaches use generative models to relax capture requirements, but still suffer from limited resolution and 4D inconsistency. To overcome these constraints, we propose RealMe, a unified framework built around a high-resolution video diffusion model that enhances limited captures into high-resolution (2K), 4D-consistent videos for volumetric video reconstruction. Specifically, RealMe constructs auxiliary data from capture videos and encodes them into latents along with layout-aware positional embeddings. The video diffusion model adapts factorized spatio-temporal attention to the multi-view capture layout, denoises these latents across viewpoints and time, and decodes them into enhanced videos to refine the 4D representation. This adaptation helps the model capture temporal dynamics and multi-view relationships, leading to more 4D-consistent generation. To reduce the data gap between generated videos and real captures, we apply a latent frequency loss that provides frequency-domain supervision in latent space. Extensive experiments on the public DNA-Rendering benchmark and our self-captured RealVV dataset demonstrate that RealMe is able to create immersive volumetric videos and outperforms state-of-the-art methods in visual fidelity and 4D consistency.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Volumetric videos capture dynamic scenes from multiple viewpoints and support free-viewpoint rendering. The immersive and interactive nature of volumetric videos makes them an effective medium for applications such as metaverse, telepresence, VR/AR, and gaming. Previous methods [Jiang et al. 2025; Pang et al. 2024; Wang et al. 2025e; Wu et al. 2024; Xu et al. 2024c] have achieved highquality volumetric video reconstruction and novel view synthesis by directly optimizing 4D scene representations. However, these approaches typically rely on dense and well-controlled capture setups that provide sufficient multi-view observations for reconstruction. This requirement makes them impractical under constrained acquisition settings, where only sparse camera arrays or low-quality input videos are available. Consequently, creating volumetric videos from limited captures while approaching the visual quality and 4D consistency of dense multi-view capture remains critical research problem and the primary motivation for our work. The central challenge is to infer global scene structure and fine details from partial observations while preserving 4D consistency. Recent work has explored using generative models [Brooks et al. 2024; Esser et al. 2024; Team Wan et al. 2025] to reduce capture requirements, leveraging their learned priors for realistic, high-quality synthesis. Some approaches [Chen et al. 2025a; Shen et al. 2024; Wu et al. 2025c] adopt two-stage optimization pipeline, using generative models to repair degraded renderings before refining the scene representation, thereby improving video resolution and frame rate. However, their generation stage treats each viewpoint independently, ignoring multi-view correlations and causing cross-view spatial inconsistency. The two-stage pipeline also introduces error accumulation between generation and reconstruction. To address this limitation, another line of work [Huang et al. 2025; Jin et al. 2025; Wu et al. 2025a] uses spatio-temporal attention during generation to facilitate information flow across spatial and temporal dimensions, producing more 4D-consistent results. Despite improved consistency, these approaches still require large-scale training data and remain limited by current generative backbones, whose native resolutions are often below 1K and therefore fall short of the visual quality required for volumetric video creation. In this paper, we propose RealMe, unified framework built around high-resolution video diffusion model that enhances limited captures into high-quality, 4D-consistent videos for subsequent SA Conference Papers 26, December 0104, 2026, Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia. volumetric video reconstruction. Specifically, given sparse and lowquality captures, RealMe first constructs auxiliary videos from input captures using diverse degradation strategies. These auxiliary videos are encoded into conditional latents, each associated with layoutaware positional embedding that describes its spatial, temporal, and latent-space information. Our video diffusion model takes these conditional latents and noise as input and decodes the denoised latents into enhanced videos. Building on prior factorized video attention [Bertasius et al. 2021], we adapt the factorization to the sampled video groups, allowing denoising to propagate information separately along the temporal and spatial dimensions rather than over flattened token sequence. As shown in Sec. 5.3.2, this adaptation improves visual fidelity and downstream 4D consistency over full attention. The generated videos and the original captures are used to optimize the scene representation [Wang et al. 2025e; Wu et al. 2024] for volumetric video reconstruction. To reduce the data gap between generated videos and real captures, we apply latent frequency loss that guides the predicted latent to preserve low-frequency structure while recovering high-frequency details. Although existing public benchmarks [Cheng et al. 2023; Isik et al. 2023] provide high-quality multi-view data, they are mostly captured in object-centric studio settings with the same focal-length multi-view camera arrays and do not fully cover long focal-length views or diverse real-world degradations. To evaluate our method under more realistic and challenging acquisition settings, we curate self-captured dataset dubbed RealVV, which contains multi-view videos with varying focal lengths, diverse scenes, actors, and performances, as well as both real and synthetic degradations. We evaluate RealMe on both the public DNA-Rendering benchmark [Cheng et al. 2023] and RealVV under limited capture settings. Extensive experiments show that RealMe is capable of creating high-quality volumetric videos and outperforms state-of-the-art methods in visual fidelity and 4D consistency. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We propose RealMe, unified framework for high-resolution 4D enhancement that reduces the capture requirements for high-quality volumetric video reconstruction. We adapt pretrained high-resolution image diffusion model [Black Forest Labs 2024] to 4D enhancement using layoutaware positional embeddings and factorized spatio-temporal attention. The adapted model is trained with latent frequency loss to reduce the data gap between generated videos and real captures. We curate RealVV, self-captured multi-view dataset with diverse degradations to support volumetric video evaluation under challenging settings and plan to release it to the community.

sections.title:
2 Related Work
2.1 Dense-View 4D Reconstruction
sections.content: Existing volumetric video reconstruction methods typically start from multi-view videos and optimize time-varying scene representation for free-viewpoint rendering. Recent systems [Li et al. 2024; Luiten et al. 2024; Wu et al. 2024; Xu et al. 2024b] model dynamic content with persistent primitives, 4D fields, or spatio-temporal features. To improve temporal scale and motion coverage, specialized representations [Jiang et al. 2025; Lei et al. 2025; Wang et al. 2025e; Xu et al. 2024c] handle long sequences, complex motion, casual videos, and human-centric topology. Other methods [Lin et al. 2024; Wang et al. 2025f; Wu et al. 2025b; Yang et al. 2024a] reduce reconstruction cost with deformation fields, dynamic particles, or lightweight monocular pipelines. Although these methods improve reconstruction quality and efficiency, they still rely on the captured frames as direct optimization evidence. Their performance therefore drops when the input views are sparse or visually degraded, which motivates an explicit enhancement stage before reconstruction.

sections.title: 2.2 Sparse-View 4D Reconstruction
sections.content: Sparse-view 4D reconstruction uses additional priors to reduce capture requirements. Geometry-aware and completion methods [Hu et al. 2025; Mihajlovic et al. 2024; Su et al. 2023; Wang et al. 2025a,d; Zhou et al. 2026] use neural fields, correspondences, monocular fusion, structured point features, flow guidance, or geometric constraints to recover structure from partial observations, including limited-view optimization and four-view capture. related sparseframe formulation [Shi et al. 2026] instead addresses temporal undersampling with texture-aware regularization. Feed-forward and generative approaches [Chen et al. 2025b; Huang et al. 2025; Jin et al. 2025; Kong et al. 2025; Liu et al. 2026; Sabathier et al. 2025; Wu et al. 2025a; Zhang et al. 2024] reduce per-scene optimization with learned reconstruction modules or use diffusion priors, including multi-view video models and transferred 3D/video priors, to synthesize missing observations and pseudo-view supervision. Human-centric approaches [Sun et al. 2025; Xiao et al. 2025; Xu et al. 2024a; Zheng et al. 2024] further reduce capture requirements by using body structure or learned human priors. These approaches make sparse capture more feasible, but they mainly solve reconstruction or category-specific rendering within fixed input setting. They do not directly address how to turn limited captured videos into higher-fidelity inputs that preserve the capture layout for general volumetric video pipeline.

sections.title: 2.3 Generative Priors for 4D Enhancement
sections.content: Generative priors offer complementary route for improving lowquality videos before they are used for reconstruction. Video restoration and super-resolution methods [Han et al. 2025; Wang et al. 2025b,c; Xu et al. 2025; Zhuang et al. 2025] use generative or diffusion models to recover realistic details, stabilize temporal changes, and handle real-world degradations. However, these models are typically designed for monocular video super-resolution, where the goal is to enhance single video stream rather than jointly enhance multi-view captures for 4D reconstruction. Several reconstruction pipelines use video models to increase effective frame rates [Chen et al. 2025a; Shen et al. 2024] or repair inferior renderings [Philip et al. 2025]. While effective, these uses of video priors remain tied to individual streams or rendered outputs rather than reconstructed representations. Other methods use image-generation models to refine reconstructed representations [Wu et al. 2025c] but are limited to static scenes. As result, they do not jointly model the camera, timestamp, and image-plane layout that determines 4D consistency RealMe: Immersive Volumetric Video from Minimal Captures across capture inputs. Large video generation and enhancement models [Brooks et al. 2024; He et al. 2024; Team Wan et al. 2025] offer strong prior for spatio-temporal synthesis, but they require layout-aware adaptation before they can be used for multi-view capture enhancement. RealMe builds on this direction by conditioning video diffusion on the 4D capture layout.

sections.title:
3 Method
3.1 Overview
sections.content: Given sparse and low-quality captures of dynamic scene, our target is to reconstruct high-quality and 4D-consistent volumetric video that supports free-viewpoint rendering. To achieve this goal, we propose RealMe, unified 4D enhancement framework. As illustrated in Fig. 2, RealMe first derives auxiliary videos from the input captures (Sec. 3.2). We then adapt the pretrained high-resolution image diffusion model [Black Forest Labs 2024] to use these auxiliary videos as conditions for generating enhanced videos for 4D reconstruction (Sec. 3.3). The detailed model architecture, including layout-aware positional embeddings and factorized spatio-temporal attention, is shown in Fig. 3. To train the model, we construct paired training examples from our self-captured dataset with diverse degradations and formulate the training objectives (Sec. 3.4).

sections.title: 3.4 Model Training and Optimization
sections.content: 3.4.1 Training Data Curation. To train the video diffusion model, we curate RealVV, high-resolution multi-view video dataset with diverse scenes, actors, performances, and camera settings, including both short-focus and long-focus views. The training split contains 100 sequences from 20 actors. Each sequence has 48 to 80 views, with 300 frames per view. In total, the training split contains over 1.4 million multi-view images. We hold out the evaluation sequences and exclude them from training. From the remaining training sequences, we construct paired training examples. Each pair contains clean target video and degraded condition video. The target provides high-resolution supervision with consistent observations, while the degraded video follows the form of the auxiliary videos used at inference time. We synthesize the degraded condition videos using three degradation strategies: (1) Sparse-view and underfit reconstruction degradation. We reconstruct coarse 4DGS from sparse views or an intentionally underfit optimization and render novel-view videos with artifacts. (2) Resolution degradation. We apply cropping, resizing, and downsampling to high-resolution videos to obtain low-resolution or ROI-limited videos. (3) Appearance and motion degradation. Following the synthetic degradation strategy of Real-ESRGAN [Wang et al. 2021], we add random noise, compression artifacts, defocus blur, and motion blur to simulate common appearance and motion degradations in real captures. Combined with the first two strategies, these perturbations approximate the artifacts present in auxiliary videos and real captures. 3.4.2 Training Objectives. sections.title: Implementation Details
sections.content: We use the DiffSynth-Studio [ModelScope Community 2024] framework for model training and inference. The pretrained base model is the 14B FLUX.1 [dev] model [Black Forest Labs 2024]. We initialize the ControlNet [Zhang et al. 2023] branch from the pretrained DiT weights and train the full branch during adaptation. During training, we use mixed temporal, spatial, and joint sampling, with detailed model and sampling configurations provided in the supplementary material. We train the model for 96 hours on 8 NVIDIA H100 GPUs with an effective batch size of 8 and learning rate of 104, and set the frequency loss weight to 0.1. To reduce memory usage, we use bfloat16 mixed-precision training and gradient checkpointing. Training target videos are generated at 2560 1440 resolution, while condition videos are resized to 1280 720 resolution. For volumetric video reconstruction, we implement the 4DGS optimization based on EasyVolcap [Xu et al. 2023]. The training settings follow FTGS [Wang et al. 2025e]. For each sequence, the final 4DGS is supervised by eight original capture views and 40 generated views enhanced from the novel-view and ROI conditions. sections.title:
5 Experiments
5.1 Settings
sections.content: 5.1.1 Datasets. We evaluate RealMe on our self-captured RealVV dataset and the public DNA-Rendering benchmark [Cheng et al. 2023]. RealVV is high-resolution multi-view video dataset containing diverse scenes, actors, performances, and camera settings, including both short-focus and long-focus cameras. We use seven sequences for evaluation, all excluded from the training data. Each evaluation sequence contains 48 views, with 180 frames per view, and is evaluated at resolution of 2560 1440. We select eight spatially distributed views as input captures and use the remaining views for novel-view evaluation. detailed analysis of input-view settings is provided in Sec. 5.3.1. DNA-Rendering [Cheng et al. 2023] contains diverse human performances with different outfits and dynamic motions. We select four sequences for zero-shot evaluation, each with 120 frames per view, and evaluate them at 10241024 resolution. We follow the same input and evaluation protocol as RealVV, using eight input views and the remaining views for novel-view evaluation. 5.1.2 Baselines. We evaluate RealMe on multiple tasks to assess its performance across several aspects. (1) Novel view synthesis measures the visual quality of rendered novel views. We use FTGS [Wang et al. 2025e] as strong 4DGS-based reconstruction baseline and DIFIX3D+ [Wu et al. 2025c] as generative baseline for novel-view enhancement. We additionally include 4C4D [Zhou et al. 2026], which is designed for four-camera sparse-view reconstruction, and 4K4D [Xu et al. 2024b], high-fidelity 4D view synthesis method. (2) 4D-consistent reconstruction tests whether the enhanced videos preserve 4D consistency for high-quality 4DGS reconstruction. We compare with Diffuman4D [Jin et al. 2025], generation-based sparseview reconstruction method. (3) Detail enhancement focuses on recovering fine appearance details from low-quality captures. We benchmark against STAR [Xie et al. 2025] and FlashVSR [Zhuang et al. 2025], two video super-resolution baselines for degraded video inputs. The implementation details and settings for the baselines are described in the supplementary material. 5.1.3 Metrics. We report PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS as quantitative metrics. PSNR and SSIM [Wang et al. 2004] measure pixel-level and structural fidelity, while LPIPS [Zhang et al. 2018] measures perceptual similarity. For 4D-consistent reconstruction, we use additional consistency metrics. Specifically, we first optimize 4DGS representation [Wang et al. 2025e] using the enhanced videos together with the input captures. We then render videos from the camera poses corresponding to the enhanced videos and compute PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS between the enhanced videos and the corresponding renderings. We use the subscript 𝑐 to denote these metrics, e.g., PSNR𝑐 . For temporal consistency, we report the optical-flow-based Temporal Warping Error (TWE) [Lai et al. 2018], which measures the residual between adjacent frames after flow-based warping over non-occluded regions; lower values indicate greater temporal stability. Because temporal smoothing can also reduce this error, we use TWE as complementary stability metric rather than measure of reconstruction fidelity. Table 1. Quantitative comparison. sections.title: 5.2 Comparison Experiments
sections.content: We compare RealMe with optimization-based and generation-based baselines under the same sparse-capture setting. Quantitative results are reported in Tab. 1, and qualitative comparisons on RealVV are shown in Fig. 5. RealMe achieves the best visual quality among all compared methods across both datasets. When optimizing the 4D representation directly from sparse input views, FTGS [Wang et al. 2025e] produces lower-quality novel views because the sparse observations provide insufficient constraints for unseen regions and view-dependent appearance. In contrast, RealMe derives scene structure from sparse input views and recovers the missing appearance. In addition to the optimization-based baseline, the generation-based baselines exhibit different limitations. DIFIX3D+ [Wu et al. 2025c] improves local details, but it does not consistently preserve the target scene appearance. Diffuman4D [Jin et al. 2025] focuses on full-body human reconstruction and therefore cannot model scene backgrounds. Due to the domain gap in its training data, it also does not generalize well to zoomed-in long-focus views in RealVV. We additionally compare with two 4D reconstruction baselines under four-camera setting on RealVV, as reported in Tab. 2. Overall, our method demonstrates stronger reconstruction performance under the four-camera setting. Compared with these optimizationbased methods, our approach leverages generative priors to recover high-frequency details missing from sparse observations and reduce artifacts caused by sparse-view inputs. We further evaluate the overall consistency between the generated videos and the input videos through downstream 4D reconstruction in Tab. 3. The results indicate that, compared with Diffuman4D [Jin et al. 2025], our generated videos better align with the input captures and lead to more coherent 4D reconstruction. These metrics are the consistency metrics defined in Sec. 5.1.3. As shown in Tab. 4, RealMe achieves temporal consistency comparable to the optimization-based baseline while outperforming the generation-based methods. In addition, we evaluate detail enhancement at 2K resolution in Fig. 6. STAR [Xie et al. 2025] and FlashVSR [Zhuang et al. 2025] improve the low-resolution inputs, but their results can still contain over-smoothed facial regions, softened hair boundaries, or artificial local textures. sections.title: 5.3 Ablation Studies
sections.content: We conduct ablation studies to assess the contribution of the model adaptations and training objective used in RealMe. We additionally vary the number of input views to analyze the trade-off between capture requirements and reconstruction quality. All ablation studies are performed on the evaluation sequences of the RealVV dataset. 5.3.1 Ablation on the Number of Input Views. As shown in Tab. 5, we evaluate RealMe with different numbers of input views to study the trade-off between capture requirements and reconstruction quality. The results show that RealMe works across the evaluated input-view settings, with substantial improvement from four to eight views and only limited additional benefits from increasing to 16 views. We therefore use eight spatially distributed views as the default setting because they provide practical balance between capture requirements and reconstruction quality. It extends the original positional IDs with temporal and spatial indices and applies factorized spatio-temporal attention along these dimensions, improving the 4D consistency of generated videos. Training further applies latent frequency loss to reduce the data gap between generated videos and real captures. Experiments on our self-captured dataset RealVV and the public DNA-Rendering benchmark [Cheng et al. 2023] show that RealMe achieves superior visual quality and 4D consistency over existing baselines, while extending volumetric video reconstruction to 2K resolution under limited capture conditions. Limitations and future work. Although RealMe achieves highquality volumetric video reconstruction with improved 4D consistency, it still has several limitations. Due to the scarcity of highquality multi-view datasets, our training data remains constrained, and the model shows limited generalization to large scenes or complex camera settings. The method may fail when the input captures provide insufficient geometric cues to initialize valid coarse 4DGS. How to scale up training data and accelerate high-resolution diffusion inference remain important directions for our future work.

sections.title: A Baseline Settings
sections.content: This section details the baseline configurations used in our evaluation. To keep the comparisons consistent, each baseline uses the same input views and frame ranges as the main experiments whenever it supports the same inputs. We rely on official implementations and released checkpoints when available, and resize the outputs to the ground-truth resolution before computing metrics. FTGS. For the 4DGS baseline, we use FTGS [Wang et al. 2025e] implemented with EasyVolcap [Xu et al. 2023]. The optimization follows the training settings of the original FTGS paper. Given the same sparse input captures as RealMe, we optimize dynamic Gaussian representation, render the held-out views, and compute novel-view metrics against the ground-truth videos. 4C4D. We use the official PyTorch implementation of 4C4D [Zhou et al. 2026] and optimize separate representation for each evaluated sequence. We use four spatially distributed input cameras and the frame range defined by the four-camera evaluation setting. Following the official pipeline, we initialize the Gaussian point cloud from the four training views with MASt3R [Leroy et al. 2024] and retain the released configuration, including 30,000 optimization iterations. We render the held-out cameras from the final checkpoint and pass the resulting full-frame images to the common novel-view evaluation pipeline. 4K4D. We evaluate 4K4D [Xu et al. 2024b] using its official EasyVolcap-based implementation and train separate model for each evaluated sequence. We adapt the released custom-dataset configuration to the calibrated RGB frames and camera parameters of RealVV, restrict the training-view list to four cameras and the corresponding evaluation frame range, and retain the official 1,600-epoch schedule and remaining model and optimization settings. After optimization, we render the held-out camera views and evaluate the full-frame outputs with the same resizing and metric computation used for the other methods. DIFIX3D+. We evaluate DIFIX3D+ [Wu et al. 2025c] as the diffusionbased enhancement baseline for sparse-view 3D reconstruction. We use the official code and checkpoint, with the released difix_ref model. For each target view, the input view with the nearest camera pose is selected as the reference view. The enhanced views are then passed to the same evaluation pipeline used by our method. Diffuman4D. We use Diffuman4D [Jin et al. 2025] as the sparseview human reconstruction baseline. This method models sparseview videos with spatio-temporal diffusion, and we evaluate it in zero-shot manner using the official code and pretrained checkpoint. Since Diffuman4D is designed for human performance reconstruction, we compute its metrics inside the foreground mask, so the evaluation focuses on the region modeled by the baseline. STAR and FlashVSR. For detail enhancement, we compare with two video super-resolution baselines, STAR [Xie et al. 2025] and FlashVSR [Zhuang et al. 2025]. We use their official code and released checkpoints, with input videos trimmed to the same frame range as our setting. Because these methods generate outputs at their default resolutions, we resize the results to the ground-truth resolution before computing PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS. Additional Implementation Details B.1 Model Architecture Our video diffusion model is built on FLUX.1 [dev] [Black Forest Labs 2024] and implemented with DiffSynth-Studio [ModelScope Community 2024]. ControlNet branch [Zhang et al. 2023] injects conditioning signals from the auxiliary videos into the diffusion model. We initialize this branch from the corresponding pretrained DiT weights, which aligns its feature scale with the base model at the start of training. During adaptation, the full ControlNet branch is trainable. For the pretrained DiT, we add rank-32 LoRA adapters [Hu et al. 2022] to the QKV projections, attention output projections, MLP layers, and modulation/projection layers, while the remaining pretrained DiT weights are frozen. In both joint and single transformer blocks, each repeated factorized-attention schedule contains three temporal attention blocks followed by one spatial attention block. We apply temporal attention more frequently because temporal modeling is more challenging than spatial modeling in our capture setting, making the 3:1 ratio practical trade-off. B.2 Training Data We provide additional details about how the degraded condition videos are synthesized. (1) For sparse-view and underfit reconstruction degradation, we either uniformly sample 32, 16, or 8 views according to camera poses to reconstruct coarse 4DGS, or train 4DGS with all views for 3,000 iterations. We then render the remaining views or all views as degraded conditions. (2) For resolution degradation, we use an offline detector [Guo and Deng 2024] to localize facial regions, pad the detected 2D boxes, and crop local ROI videos. For blur/resize-based low-resolution generation, we apply USM sharpening and first-stage blur with kernel sizes from 7 to 21. We sample the configured blur-kernel types with probabilities [0.45, 0.25, 0.12, 0.03, 0.12, 0.03], perform stochastic resizing, and use bicubic upsampling to produce 1280 720 condition videos. (3) For appearance and motion degradation, we follow the degradation design of Real-ESRGAN [Wang et al. 2021] and add random noise, compression artifacts, defocus blur, and motion blur. Together, these degradations cover geometry artifacts, resolution loss, local detail loss, appearance noise, and motion blur. B.3 Training Strategy Condition videos are fixed at 1280 720 resolution during training. For target videos, we use progressive resolution schedule that increases from 1280720 to 25601440. This schedule stabilizes highresolution training, while the final training stage remains consistent with the 25601440 target resolution reported in the main paper. Runtime Peak Memory 135.1 48.1 GB Additional Qualitative Results C.1 Qualitative Comparisons We provide additional qualitative comparisons on RealVV and DNARendering [Cheng et al. 2023]. These examples extend the main paper results to more sequences and viewpoints, covering novel view synthesis, detail enhancement, and 4D-consistent reconstruction under the same limited-capture setting. As shown in Fig. 7, RealMe preserves both foreground motion and scene background across diverse camera views, while the baselines either lose scene content or introduce visible appearance artifacts. We also test zero-shot generalization on DNA-Rendering [Cheng et al. 2023] in Fig. 8. The examples cover two unseen performers at different timestamps and held-out viewpoints, complementing the quantitative comparison in the main paper. Across these settings, RealMe preserves each performers appearance and motion structure while remaining close to the ground truth. We also provide focused comparison on zoomed-in long-focus views in Fig. 9. These views are challenging because sparse captures provide weak constraints for fine-scale appearance and background regions. The comparison shows that the generated views and the reconstructed results from RealMe remain closer to the ground truth than the optimization-based and generation-based baselines. C.2 High-Resolution Detail Comparisons We include high-resolution detail comparisons on RealVV. Each example presents the full-frame result together with zoomed-in crops, making facial details, clothing textures, and local motion details easier to inspect. These comparisons complement the quantitative detail enhancement metrics in the main paper. C.3 Qualitative Ablation Results We provide qualitative ablation results for layout-aware positional embedding, factorized spatio-temporal attention, and latent frequency loss. These visual comparisons complement the ablation tables in the main paper by showing how each component affects local detail quality and 4D consistency across time and views. In Fig. 10, we visualize the effect of latent frequency loss in both RGB space and latent frequency space. The low-frequency maps capture coarse structure, while the high-frequency maps highlight local texture and boundary details. With latent frequency loss, the generated results retain sharper high-frequency structures and reduce visible detail errors.
